title: What Is an RFI? A Clear Guide to Request for Information, With Examples
summary: An RFI is a request for information. See how buyers use RFIs to research vendors, how construction RFIs differ, and how vendors should respond.
body_markdown:
An RFI is a request for information. It is a formal document one party sends another to gather facts before making a decision. The abbreviation carries two distinct meanings in US business, and they belong to different processes:


- **In procurement** , a buyer issues an RFI to potential vendors early in the sourcing process, before any proposal or pricing request, to learn what solutions exist and which suppliers are capable.
- **In construction** , a contractor submits an RFI to the architect, engineer, or owner during a project to clarify drawings, specifications, or site conditions.


This guide explains both. It also covers what belongs in an RFI, how RFI differs from RFP and RFQ, and how vendors should decide whether and how to respond.


### **Key Takeaways**


- An RFI (request for information) is a document used to gather facts before a decision. It has two common uses:[procurement](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/procurement-rfis-request-for-information) and construction.
- In procurement, a buyer sends an RFI to vendors early, before an RFP or RFQ, to learn what solutions and suppliers exist.
- In construction, a contractor sends an RFI to the design team to clarify drawings, specs, or site conditions during a project.
- An RFI is not a bid and is not binding. Responding creates no obligation, and no award follows directly from it.
- In the sourcing sequence, an RFI comes before the[RFP](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/what-is-a-request-for-proposal-rfp) (full proposal) and the RFQ (firm pricing).


## RFI in Procurement: The Buyer's Research Document


A procurement RFI is market research in document form. The buyer knows it has a problem but does not yet know the full range of solutions, the capable suppliers, or sometimes even the right requirements. So it asks the market before it asks for proposals.


A well-built RFI requests facts a buyer can compare: company background, relevant experience, solution capabilities, compliance credentials such as SOC 2 or ISO certifications, integration options, and implementation approach. It does not request detailed pricing or a full proposed solution. Those belong to the RFQ and RFP stages that may follow.


### What happens after an RFI


The buyer compares responses, refines its requirements based on what it learned, and typically shortlists vendors for the next stage. Three outcomes are common:


1. **An**[RFP](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/rfp-request-for-proposal-your-ultimate-guide-to-rfps) **follows.** The buyer now understands the market and asks shortlisted vendors for full proposals.
2. **An RFQ follows.** The buyer's requirement turned out to be a defined product or service, so it goes straight to pricing.
3. **Nothing follows.** The research showed the project is premature, too expensive, or already solved internally. This outcome is normal, and vendors should factor it into how much effort a response deserves.

## RFI in Construction: How Contractors Get Answers On-Site


A construction RFI works differently. It is a formal, logged question from the contractor to the design team when the drawings, specifications, or site conditions leave something unclear, missing, or contradictory. The answer becomes part of the project record, and if it changes cost or schedule, it can trigger a change order.


The volume is larger than most people outside the industry expect. The widely cited[Navigant Construction Forum study](https://www.cmaanet.org/sites/default/files/2018-04/NCF%20IMPACT%20%26%20CONTROL%20OF%20RFIs%20ON%20CONSTRUCTION%20PROJECTS.pdf) of 1,362 projects and more than one million RFIs found an average of 796 RFIs per project, an average cost of about $1,080 to review and respond to each one, and an average first reply time of 6.4 days. On a typical project, that adds up to hundreds of thousands of dollars in administrative cost, which is why construction teams invest in RFI logs, standard formats, and response deadlines.


A good construction RFI states the exact location, references the specific drawing or spec section, asks one clear question, and proposes a solution the designer can confirm or reject. Our overview of the[different types of construction RFIs](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/different-types-rfi-construction) breaks down the main categories.


## Key Components of an RFI and How Issuers Write One


### The components


A complete RFI contains seven parts:


1. **Basic request details.** Issuer name, RFI title and reference number, issue date, response deadline, and a contact for questions.
2. **Statement of purpose.** What decision the information will support and why the organization is going to market now.
3. **Company background.** A short profile of the issuer so vendors can tailor their responses to the size and industry involved.
4. **Project summary and scope.** The problem, the current environment, known constraints, and the approximate scale.
5. **Information requested.** Structured questions covering company profile, relevant experience, solution capabilities, compliance credentials, integration options, implementation approach, and pricing model. Each question should map to something the buyer will evaluate.
6. **Response instructions.** Format, submission method, page limit, and deadline. A standard response template keeps answers comparable.
7. **Next steps.** What follows the RFI, and when respondents will hear back.


### The writing process, step by step


1. **Define the decision first.** Write down what you need to decide after reading the responses. Every question earns its place by serving that decision.
2. **Draft the seven components** , keeping the question list short. Twenty focused questions produce better responses than fifty broad ones.
3. **Prescreen the distribution list.** Sending an RFI to every vendor in the category produces a pile of responses nobody can process. Target vendors that plausibly fit.
4. **Send it with a response template and a realistic deadline.** Two to three weeks is a reasonable floor for a substantive RFI.
5. **Evaluate consistently and close the loop.** Score responses against the same criteria, notify respondents of the outcome, and record what you learned for the RFP stage.


A ready-made structure speeds this up. Our[RFI template](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/rfi-template-word) provides the full document skeleton.


## RFI Example


Here is a condensed procurement RFI that shows the components in use.


Request for Information: Customer Support Platform


Issued by:


Regional insurance provider, ~2,000 employees | RFI-2026-014 | Responses due: 3 weeks from issue


Purpose:


We are researching cloud customer support platforms for three call centers with roughly 400 agents, replacing a legacy on-premise system. Responses will inform an RFP planned for next quarter.


Scope specifics:


Cloud deployment required. Must integrate with Salesforce and our existing telephony system. HIPAA compliance is mandatory. Rollout would be phased across three sites.


Information requested:


Company profile and years in market. Platform capabilities against the scope above. Compliance certifications with audit dates. Integration approach for the named systems. Typical implementation timeline for a deployment of this size. Pricing model (a description of how you charge, not a quote).


Response instructions:


Maximum 10 pages, submitted through the portal linked below. Questions by email during week one; answers will be shared with all recipients.


Next steps:


Shortlisted vendors will be notified within two weeks of the deadline and invited to the RFP.

## Why RFIs Are Valuable


An RFI is cheap and fast: one document and a few weeks. It saves you from spending the far more expensive RFP and[RFQ](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/rfq) stages on vendors that were never a fit. An RFI delivers this value in five ways:


- **It reduces vendor-selection risk early.** Compliance credentials, certifications such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001, and financial stability get verified before any vendor reaches the expensive RFP stage.
- **It sharpens the requirements.** Responses reveal capabilities, constraints, and options the buyer did not know existed, so the eventual RFP asks better questions.
- **It narrows the field cheaply.** Evaluating a full proposal takes real hours on both sides. An RFI filters a long vendor list down to the few worth that effort.
- **It creates an audit trail.** Documented market research supports due diligence and shows regulators, auditors, or leadership why the shortlist looks the way it does. Public-sector buyers are often required to produce exactly this record.
- **It maps the market.** Even when no purchase follows, the buyer learns current pricing models, technology directions, and which suppliers are investing in the category.


For vendors, the RFI is an opportunity, not a chore. Because the buyer has not finalized its requirements yet, a clear response that explains your approach can influence the RFP that every competitor will later have to answer. Getting your strengths written into the buyer's evaluation criteria at this stage is worth more than a polished proposal after the requirements are locked.


## RFI vs. RFP vs. RFQ


The three documents form a sequence from least to most commitment. The[US General Services Administration](https://www.gsa.gov/small-business/training-and-events/rfis-rfqs-and-rfps) uses the same three-way distinction in its guidance for federal vendors.


Document The buyer is asking Vendor effort to respond Binding?


RFI (Request for Information) "What exists, and who can do this?" Low to moderate No


RFP (Request for Proposal) "Propose your full solution, team, and price." High Response terms often carry into contract


RFQ (Request for Quotation) "Price this defined requirement." Low to moderate Quotes are typically firm


Two clarifications prevent most confusion. First, an RFI is not a bid: responding creates no obligation on either side, and no award follows directly from it. Second, RFQ has a second expansion, request for qualifications, used in construction and professional services to prescreen firms. Read the document itself rather than assuming from the abbreviation. Our guide to the[differences between RFI, RFQ, and RFP](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/differences-between-rfi-rfq-rfp) covers when buyers use each.

## For Vendors: How to Decide Whether an RFI Is Worth Answering


Most guides cover RFIs from the buyer's side only. If you sell for a living, the harder questions are whether to respond and how much effort to spend. Use these tests:


- **Check what the RFI feeds.** In[government contracting](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/writing-government-contract-proposals-ai) , an RFI or Sources Sought response can influence whether the eventual contract is set aside for small businesses and how the requirement is written. That influence makes responding valuable even without a direct award. A purely informational commercial RFI with no budget behind it deserves a leaner response.
- **Answer the questions asked, not the questions you wish were asked.** Generic capability statements read as marketing and get skimmed. Map your answers to the issuer's structure, and where the RFI includes a statement of work, respond task by task.
- **Handle the no-questions RFI deliberately.** Some RFIs, especially federal ones, provide a scope but no explicit questions. Respond with a short company profile, your relevant experience mapped against the scope, and your contract vehicles or certifications. Contact the listed point of contact if an attachment seems to be missing.
- **Follow up once, briefly.** Silence after an RFI response is normal, particularly in government. Confirm receipt with the point of contact, then monitor for the follow-on solicitation rather than sending repeated messages.
- **Reuse your answers.** RFIs across buyers ask overlapping questions about your company, security, and capabilities. A maintained answer library turns each response from a writing project into an assembly job. Our guide on[writing an effective RFI response](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/write-effective-rfi-response) covers structure and content in detail.


## Best Practices for Issuing an RFI


For buyers, the quality of RFI responses is set by the quality of the RFI. These five practices produce responses you can actually compare, and each carries a note for the vendors reading them.


### 1. State the problem, not the presumed solution


Describe the business problem, the current environment, and the outcome you need. Naming a specific solution too early narrows the market research the RFI exists to perform. **For vendors:** when a buyer describes a problem openly, your response can shape their requirements. No later stage of the sales cycle offers that much influence.


### 2. Ask questions you will actually evaluate


Every question should map to a decision criterion. Question lists padded with nice-to-know items lower response quality across the board, because vendors budget effort by total length. **For vendors:** answer every question, even briefly. Skipped questions read as capability gaps.


### 3. Do not ask for detailed pricing


An RFI precedes defined requirements, so any detailed pricing you collect will be built on vendor guesses. Ask instead for pricing models and rough ranges if you need budget guidance. **For vendors:** if an RFI demands firm pricing, flag your assumptions explicitly. Unstated assumptions become expectations later.


### 4. Give a standard response format and a realistic deadline


A fixed structure makes responses comparable, and two to three weeks is a reasonable floor for a substantive RFI. **For vendors:** matching the requested format exactly is the cheapest credibility signal available.


### 5. Tell vendors what happens next


State whether a shortlist, an RFP, or a decision timeline follows, and inform respondents of the outcome. Vendors remember buyers who close the loop, and the next RFI from that buyer gets better responses. **For vendors:** if the RFI states no next step, ask about one in your response. The answer tells you how much this opportunity is worth.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **Is an RFI legally binding?**


No. A procurement RFI creates no obligation for the buyer to purchase or for the vendor to bid, and responses are not offers. Construction RFIs differ: the documented answers become part of the project record and can support or trigger contract changes, so their content carries contractual weight even though the RFI itself is a question.


### **Can an RFI include pricing questions?**


It can, but well-run RFIs ask for pricing models or indicative ranges rather than firm quotes. Requirements are not defined yet at the RFI stage, so any detailed pricing rests on vendor assumptions. Firm pricing belongs in the RFQ or RFP that follows.


### **What is a Sources Sought notice, and is it the same as an RFI?**


Both are federal market-research tools posted on SAM.gov, and agencies often use the labels interchangeably. A Sources Sought notice specifically asks which businesses can perform the work, and the responses inform set-aside decisions, such as whether the contract is reserved for small businesses. For a small business, that makes responding strategically important even though no award is attached.


### **How should a vendor respond to an RFI that contains no questions?**


Build your own structure. Open with a short company profile, then map your capabilities against each element of the stated scope or statement of work, and close with certifications, contract vehicles, and a point of contact. Before submitting, check with the issuer whether a question attachment was omitted from the posting.


### **Should a vendor follow up after submitting an RFI response?**


Once, briefly. A short message confirming receipt is appropriate, especially in government contracting where acknowledgment is rare. After that, track the opportunity and watch for the follow-on solicitation instead of sending repeated follow-ups. Silence usually means the research phase is simply not finished.


### **Who answers an RFI in construction?**


The design team, typically the architect or the engineer of record, depending on the discipline the question touches. The owner gets involved when the answer affects cost, schedule, or scope. The contractor who submitted the RFI then reviews the response and, if it changes the work, initiates the change management process.
